title: Suppliers both systems agree on
prompt: The supplier list comes from two systems. Write `solve(suppliers)` so it returns the suppliers whose two records are exactly the same in both systems.
rules: Each system lists a supplier at most once; `source_system` says which system a row comes from.
A supplier qualifies when both systems list it and every other column is equal. Two missing values count as equal.
A supplier listed by only one system, or with any difference between its two records, is left out.
Return `supplier_id`, `supplier_name`, `country`, `payment_terms_days` and `contact_email`, one row per qualifying supplier.
hints: Leave out `source_system` and select the other five columns. A supplier the systems agree on now appears as two identical rows.
`distinct()` keeps one copy of each row. What is left if you take those copies away from the full list, counting repeats?
`exceptAll` removes one copy per matching row, so `details.exceptAll(details.distinct())` keeps exactly the second copies. `subtract` would remove everything.
explanation: Drop `source_system` so the two records of a supplier can be compared: `details = suppliers.select("supplier_id", "supplier_name", "country", "payment_terms_days", "contact_email")`. A supplier both systems agree on is now a repeated row; one with any difference is two different rows, and one listed once is a single row. `details.exceptAll(details.distinct())` takes one copy of every row away and leaves only the second copies. Set operations treat two missing values as equal, so a supplier missing the same field in both systems still matches. Filtering each system and using `intersect` on the five columns gives the same rows. `subtract` in place of `exceptAll` removes every copy and returns nothing.
